Anaesthesia doctors in training carried out the procedure under the supervision of experienced doctors. We compared two methods: using a video camera to help guide the tube or looking directly into the mouth and throat. WHY WE DID IT: Placing a breathing tube can be difficult. Using a video camera may help doctors see the opening to the windpipe more clearly and make it easier to place the tube correctly. We wanted to find out whether this method worked better when used by anaesthesi

items.title: Preoperative Oral Esketamine for Perioperative Comfort in Children Undergoing Adenotonsillectomy: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Dose-Finding Study.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Pediatric adenotonsillectomy often causes preoperative anxiety, venous cannulation pain, and emergence agitation. Esketamine has multimodal properties, but the optimal oral dose for children is unknown. This study evaluated oral esketamine at 1, 2, and 3 mg/kg for perioperative comfort. METHODS: In this randomized double-blind trial, 99 children (ASA I-II, 1-6 years) received oral 10% glucose (control, n = 26) or esketamine 1 mg/kg (EK1, n = 26), 2 mg/kg (EK2, n = 23), or 3 mg/kg (EK3, n = 24) 30 min before anesthesia. PRIMARY OUTCOMES: Ramsay Sedation Scale (RSS) and FLACC pain score at venous cannulation, and PAED score at 15 min after extubation. SECONDARY OUTCOMES: remifentanil use, postoperative FLACC (2-48 h), sleep quality, and adverse events. RESULTS: All esketamine doses improved sedation and analgesia at cannulation (overall p < 0.001), with largest effect at 3 mg/kg. Median RSS (IQR): control 1.00 (1.00-2.00); EK1 2.00 (1.75-3.00, p = 0.028); EK2 2.00 (1.00-3.00, p = 0.049); EK3 3.00 (2.00-3.37, p < 0.001). FLACC scores: control 6.00 (3.00-7.00); EK1 2.50 (1.00-4.00, p = 0.016); EK2 2.00 (0.00-4.00, p = 0.001); EK3 0.00 (0.00-1.75, p < 0.001). PAED score at 15 min was lower in EK2 than control (5.00 [2.00-10.00] vs. 10.00 [6.00-12.00], p = 0.048). Remifentanil consumption was reduced in EK3 (120.00 [80.00-159.50] vs. 240.00 [160.00-315.00] μg, p = 0.001). Postoperative pain at 2-6 h was lower in EK2 and EK3 (p < 0.05), persisting to 48 h in EK3 (p < 0.05). Sleep quality improved in EK3 at 24 h (p = 0.023) and 48 h (p = 0.032). Adverse events did not differ significantly. CONCLUSIONS: Preoperative oral esketamine (1-3 mg/kg) enhances perioperative comfort in children undergoing adenotonsillectomy. The 2 mg/kg dose offers the best balance of efficacy and safety, while 3 mg/kg provides superior analgesia and opioid sparing.

items.title: EEG-Guided Sevoflurane Anesthesia and Emergence Delirium in Children: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: In pediatric anesthesia, minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) guides inhalational agent dosing but may not accurately reflect anesthetic depth. EEG-guided anesthesia has shown benefits in adults but remains underused in children. AIMS: This study aims to evaluate the effect of EEG-guided anesthesia with SedLine on emergence delirium (ED) and sevoflurane dose in behaviorally noncompliant children undergoing dental procedures under general anesthesia. METHODS: In this prospective, randomized controlled trial, 100 children aged 4-10 years were randomized to standard anesthesia guided by MAC and conventional clinical signs (standard group) or EEG-guided anesthesia titrated to SedLine parameters (primary target: PSI 25-50; secondary parameter: SEF 10-15 Hz) (EEG-S group). Primary outcome was ED incidence assessed by the Pediatric Anesthesia Emergence Delirium Scale (PAEDS). Secondary outcomes included mean EtSevo values, postoperative pain, rescue analgesia, nausea/vomiting, recovery time. RESULTS: Median PAEDS scores during the first 120 min postoperatively were significantly lower in the EEG-S group compared with the Standard group (e.g., upon arrival to PACU: 4 [IQR 4] vs. 8 [IQR 4.5]). In addition, the incidence of ED upon arrival in the recovery room was significantly lower in the EEG-S group (17% vs. 43%) and at 10 min postoperatively (17% vs. 37%). The mean end-tidal sevoflurane concentration was statistically lower in the EEG-S group (maintenance EtSevo 1.88 ± 0.25 vs. 1.98 ± 0.20; mean difference = 0.10, 95% confidence interval: 0.006-0.190; p = 0.036). Postoperative FLACC pain scores were also lower in the EEG-S group, representing a potential confounding factor for ED outcomes. CONCLUSION: EEG-guided anesthesia was associated with lower PAEDS scores and reduced sevoflurane consumption compared with standard management. However, given small EEG-derived differences and potential confounding by postoperative pain, these findings should be interpreted cautiously. Within the applied target ranges, EEG-derived parameters were not independently associated with ED, and specific EEG targets predictive of ED could not be identified. TRIAL REGISTRATION: This study was registered (Protocol Registration Receipt NCT06400706/OKocaturk/May 02 2024) at http://www. CLINICALTRIAL: gov.

items.title: Automated Versus Manual Endotracheal Tube Cuff Pressure Control in Mechanically Ventilated Children: A Randomized Crossover Trial.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Optimal endotracheal tube cuff pressure is key for airway sealing and minimizing microaspiration and tracheal injury in ventilated children. However, intermittent manual monitoring can allow significant pressure changes and be affected by measurement artifacts, potentially reducing airway protection. AIMS: This study evaluated whether automated cuff pressure control better maintains target pressure than manual monitoring in ventilated children, and assessed its effects on off-target pressure and workload. METHODS: In this prospective, randomized crossover study, mechanically ventilated pediatric patients (1 month-18 years) expected to require ventilation for ≥ 48 h underwent two randomized 24-h monitoring phases (manual and automated). During the manual phase, cuff pressure was continuously displayed via a closed system without repeated disconnection of the manometer and was intermittently adjusted by bedside nurses according to a predefined protocol. During the automated phase, cuff pressure was continuously regulated using an automated control system to maintain a target range of 15-25 cmH2O. The primary outcomes were the frequency and cumulative duration of off-target cuff pressure exposure; secondary outcomes included nursing workload. RESULTS: Thirty-two patients completed both phases (768 measurements). Low cuff pressure episodes (< 15 cmH2O) were more frequent during manual monitoring than automated monitoring (12.7% vs. 1.3%, p < 0.001), while high-pressure episodes (> 25 cmH2O) occurred only during manual monitoring (2.6% vs. 0%, p < 0.001). Total time outside the target range was markedly reduced with automated monitoring (118 vs. 10 h, p < 0.001). Nursing workload was significantly lower in the automated phase (3.65 h vs. 0.08 h, p < 0.001). CONCLUSIONS: Automated cuff pressure control more reliably maintains target pressure and minimizes clinically important deviations compared to manual management. These results support adopting continuous automated regulation as a preferred strategy to enhance airway safety and reduce workload in mechanically ventilated children. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06965400).

items.title: Sugammadex versus neostigmine for neuromuscular blockade reversal in adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Reversal of neuromuscular blockade (NMB) is a routine component of general anaesthesia with important implications for recovery quality and peri-operative safety. Recent changes in the cost of sugammadex, together with its efficacy and adverse effect profile relative to neostigmine, may influence its broader clinical use. OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of sugammadex compared with neostigmine in adult patients. DESIGN: Systematic review of randomised controlled trials with meta-analyses and trial sequential analyses. Certainty of evidence was assessed using the Grades of Recommendation, Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) framework. This is an update of a 2017 Cochrane review. DATA SOURCES: Online databases were searched up to December 2025. ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: Randomised trials enrolling adults receiving rocuronium or vecuronium for elective procedures and comparing sugammadex with neostigmine were included. The outcomes included NMB recovery time and risk of various adverse events. RESULTS: We included 165 trials with 19 124 participants. Risk of bias was generally unclear or high. NMB monitoring technique was reported in 113 trials, mostly acceleromyography. Time to reversal of NMB from second twitch to a train-of-four ratio more than 0.9 was shorter with sugammadex 2 mg kg-1 versus neostigmine 0.05 mg kg-1 (mean difference = -10.49 min (95% confidence interval, -11.90 to -9.08), GRADE: moderate). Sugammadex probably reduces the number of patients with at least one adverse event compared with neostigmine (risk ratio = 0.72 (95% confidence interval, 0.61 to 0.84), GRADE: moderate). When looking at specific adverse events, sugammadex probably reduces the risk of residual NMB, inadequate NMB reversal, desaturation, atelectasis, increased upper airway secretion, airway obstruction, bradycardia, dry mouth and urinary retention (GRADE: moderate). CONCLUSIONS: Sugammadex probably reverses NMB more rapidly and with fewer adverse events than neostigmine. Broader use of sugammadex has the potential to improve peri-operative outcomes.

items.title: Pre-Extubation Low-Dose Propofol in Pediatric Ear, Nose, and Throat Procedures: A Meta-Analysis With Trial Sequential Analysis.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Post-extubation emergence agitation (EA) is common in pediatric ear, nose, and throat (ENT) procedures and may lead to serious complications. AIMS: To assess the efficacy of low-dose propofol administered before extubation, compared with placebo, for preventing EA, using meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis (TSA). METHODS: We searched PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing low-dose propofol versus placebo administered before extubation in pediatric ENT procedures. The primary outcomes were laryngospasm, severity of EA, assessed by the Pediatric Anesthesia Emergence Delirium (PAED) scale score, and incidence of EA. Secondary outcomes included post-anesthesia care unit (PACU) length of stay, time to recovery, and time to extubation. Random-effects models were used to pool effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). TSA was performed for all outcomes to assess the robustness of the evidence. RESULTS: Ten RCTs were included in the review, of which six (414 pediatric patients) contributed to the meta-analysis. Compared with control, propofol significantly reduced the incidence of EA (risk ratio [RR] = 0.57; 95% CI, 0.42-0.78) and lowered agitation severity (mean difference [MD] = -3.94; 95% CI, -5.74 to -2.13). Time to extubation was slightly longer (MD = 1.8 min; 95% CI, 1.4-2.3), whereas time to recovery (MD = 0.9 min; 95% CI, -1.9 to 3.6) and PACU length of stay (MD = -0.63 min; 95% CI, -3.2 to 1.9) did not differ. TSA confirmed the robustness of the findings for incidence of EA, severity of EA, and time to extubation. However, the certainty of evidence was very low for severity of EA and moderate for EA incidence and time to extubation. Laryngospasm outcomes were not pooled due to substantial heterogeneity. CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that pre-extubation propofol probably reduces the incidence of EA in pediatric ENT surgery, supported by moderate-certainty evidence, and may lower EA severity measured by PAED scale scores, for which the certainty of evidence was very low. Propofol was also associated with a slightly longer time to extubation, with no difference in overall recovery time or PACU length of stay.

items.title: Effects of Esketamine on Emergence Delirium in Children Undergoing Sevoflurane Anesthesia: A Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis, and Trial Sequential Analysis.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Emergence delirium is a frequent and distressing postoperative complication in children, particularly following sevoflurane-based anesthesia. Despite its clinical importance, the optimal preventive strategy remains under investigation. This study aims to systematically evaluate the efficacy and safety of esketamine in preventing emergence delirium in pediatric patients undergoing sevoflurane-based general anesthesia. METHODS: We systematically searched seven databases and registries through 27 March 2026. Randomized controlled trials that compared esketamine with placebo in children undergoing surgical procedures were included. The primary outcome was the incidence of emergence delirium. Secondary outcomes were postoperative pain scores, extubation time, post-anesthesia care unit stay, and postoperative nausea and vomiting. Data were synthesized using random-effects models, with risk ratios for dichotomous outcomes and mean differences or standardized mean differences for continuous outcomes. Meta-regression and trial sequential analysis were performed. The risk of bias was assessed using the revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomized trials, and the certainty of the evidence was evaluated using the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation approach. RESULTS: Eight randomized controlled trials involving 916 patients were included. Esketamine significantly reduced the incidence of emergence delirium versus placebo (risk ratio = 0.35; 95% confidence interval: 0.26-0.48; p < 0.0001). No significant differences were observed between dosing regimens, surgical types, routes of administration, or timing of administration. Pain scores were significantly lower with esketamine (standardized mean difference = -0.58; 95% confidence interval: -0.79 to -0.37; p < 0.0001). Extubation time was modestly prolonged (mean difference = 1.72 min; 95% confidence interval: 0.20-3.24; p = 0.0267). Meta-regression revealed a statistically significant association between emergence delirium risk ratios and anesthesia duration (β = 0.98, p = 0.042), with no other significant associations observed for the other covariates. items.title: Childhood Exposure to General Anesthesia for Surgery: Identification of a Subtle Postoperative Cognitive Phenotype.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Early-life exposure to general anesthesia has not been consistently associated with overall cognitive deficits, yet its impact on executive functions and visuo-spatial processing remains unclear. The primary objective was to assess executive function performance, according to general anesthesia exposure for surgery. The secondary objectives were to explore distinct cognitive profiles and their associated factors, as well as to examine visuo-spatial attention as a complementary domain. METHODS: In this ambidirectional cohort study, 77 children aged 9 to 11 yr, with or without previous general anesthesia exposure for surgery, completed a cognitive battery yielding eight cognitive measures assessing inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility, working memory, and visuo-spatial attention. Measures were analyzed using a linear mixed-effects model. Exploratory latent profile analysis was used to identify cognitive performance profiles. RESULTS: No significant main effect of general anesthesia exposure for surgery was observed (chi-square[1] = 0.01; P = 0.92), indicating comparable overall executive function performance between exposed (mean age at exposure, 4.47 ± 3.00 yr) and nonexposed. Latent profile analysis identified two executive function profiles: efficient and vulnerable executive control. General anesthesia exposure was associated with slightly higher odds of belonging to the vulnerable profile group (odds ratio, 1.16; 95% CI; 1.151 to 1.159; P < 0.001). Regarding visuo-spatial attention, general anesthesia-exposed participants showed higher global-local precedence measures (estimate, 0.53; 95% CI, 0.04 to 1.01; P = 0.036). CONCLUSIONS: Early childhood exposure to general anesthesia was not associated with reduced overall executive function. However, a potential postoperative cognitive phenotype is suggested by a higher likelihood to belonging to a vulnerable executive control profile, together with greater visuo-spatial global-local precedence.

items.title: Comparing Subglottic Ultrasound and Distal Phalanx Width for Pediatric Endotracheal Tube Sizing in a Predominantly School-Aged Pediatric Cohort: A Prospective Study.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Accurate endotracheal tube (ETT) sizing is essential in pediatric airway management to optimize ventilation and reduce complications. Traditional methods, including age-based formulas and distal phalanx width (DPW), may lack precision. Subglottic ultrasound (US) has emerged as a promising tool, but its predictive accuracy compared with DPW remains unclear. This study aimed to compare accuracy, agreement, diagnostic performance, and clinical applicability of subglottic US versus DPW for predicting optimal ETT size in children, while recognizing that the enrolled cohort was predominantly school-aged. METHODS: In this prospective observational study, pediatric patients aged 0-12 years undergoing elective or emergency intubation were assessed. Pre-intubation measurements included subglottic transverse airway diameter by ultrasound (ACUSON Juniper, microconvex probe, 5-10 MHz) and DPW by digital calipers. Predicted ETT sizes were compared with the final clinically accepted cuffed ETT inner diameter confirmed by leak testing and cuff pressure optimization. Agreement was evaluated using Bland-Altman analysis and intraclass correlation coefficients, while diagnostic performance was defined a priori as accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), likelihood ratios, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis. Logistic regression identified predictors of good ETT fit. RESULTS: Among 160 patients, the median age was 8.8 years (IQR 7.0-10.5), indicating predominance of older children. Ultrasound-predicted ETT size showed a stronger correlation with actual size (r = 0.479, p < 0.001) than DPW (r = 0.248, p = 0.002). Ultrasound predictions had narrower Bland-Altman limits of agreement, although ultrasound measurement is operator-dependent. DPW showed poor sensitivity (5.9%) but high specificity (99.3%) for identifying underfit ETTs, with limited overall discrimination (ROC AUC = 0.53). Only subglottic diameter was a significant predictor of good ETT fit. CONCLUSION: Subglottic ultrasound showed better agreement with clinically accepted ETT size than DPW in this predominantly school-aged pediatric cohort. These findings support the potential role of ultrasound as an adjunct to pediatric airway assessment, but conclusions should be interpreted cautiously in infants and younger children because they were under-represented. Standardized measurement protocols and operator training are needed

items.title: Effects of Different Measures for the Treatment of Arterial Hypotension on Cerebral Oxygen Saturation During Pediatric General Anesthesia: An Observational Pilot Study.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Intraoperative hypotension is a common complication in pediatric anesthesia. The definition of hypotension and treatment strategies are heterogeneous. The association of these treatments with cerebral regional oxygen saturation, measured by near-infrared spectroscopy, is insufficiently characterized. AIMS: The study explores whether changes in cerebral regional oxygen saturation, mean arterial pressure, and heart rate differ after the administration of an isotonic fluid bolus, noradrenaline, adrenaline, or cafedrine/theodrenaline for perioperative hypotension in children. METHODS: This single-center, observational pilot study included children aged 18 years or younger undergoing noncardiac surgery who developed hypotension requiring treatment. The choice of the intervention was at the discretion of the attending anesthetist and guided by an internal guideline. Cerebral regional oxygen saturation, mean arterial pressure, and heart rate were recorded for 8 min after the first intervention and analyzed relative to the value immediately before treatment. Groups were compared using the area under the curve of these changes and linear mixed-effects models. RESULTS: Forty-six patients were analyzed. Cerebral regional oxygen saturation immediately before treatment did not differ from the pre-induction baseline. Cafedrine/theodrenaline was the only treatment associated with a sustained increase in cerebral regional oxygen saturation, with a significantly higher area under the curve than noradrenaline (p = 0.017), adrenaline (p = 0.017), and fluid administration (p < 0.001), which was confirmed by mixed-effects models. Only cafedrine/theodrenaline was associated with an increase in heart rate. Changes in heart rate were significantly correlated with changes in cerebral regional oxygen saturation (Spearman's ρ = 0.376, p = 0.010), but not with changes in mean arterial pressure. CONCLUSIONS: Cafedrine/theodrenaline was associated with a sustained increase in cerebral regional oxygen saturation, heart rate, and blood pressure. Noradrenaline, adrenaline, and fluid administration were associated with unchanged or decreasing cerebral regional oxygen saturation. Randomized controlled studies are required to confirm these findings.

items.title: A Pilot and Feasibility Study of a Four-Stage Neurological Staging Framework in Pediatric Tracheal Extubation During Anesthesia Emergence.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Postoperative tracheal extubation is a particularly high-risk period in pediatric anesthesia. Because emergence from anesthesia is a complex and complicated process, determining the optimal timing for safe tracheal extubation remains challenging. AIMS: To evaluate the feasibility and descriptive characteristics of a four-stage neuroanatomical framework for pediatric anesthesia emergence while providing exploratory incidence estimates of respiratory adverse events across these stages. METHODS: Children younger than 7 years undergoing general anesthesia were enrolled. Emergence stratified into four stages, defined by cranial nerve indicators: Stage 1 (Medulla: regular breathing, movement, excluding cough or swallowing); Stage 2 (Pons: tearing or grimacing); Stage 3 (Midbrain: conjugate gaze or eye-opening); and Stage 4 (Cerebrum: purposeful movement). Primary outcomes included feasibility metrics-such as protocol completion, recruitment flow, and data completeness-and successful assignment of emergence stages. Exploratory descriptive statistics summarized the incidence of respiratory adverse events. Risk ratios were calculated to compare the occurrence of respiratory adverse events in intermediate (Stages 2 and 3) and cortical (Stage 4) stages. RESULTS: Of the 174 patients screened, 89 completed the protocol. Overall, 153 patients provided consent (91.6% consent rate). The overall data capture rate was 58.2% (89/153), while the worksheet processing rate-adjusted for protocol-ineligible cases, such as those with supraglottic airway use-was 73.2% (112/153). Among the 89 patients analyzed, there were no missing data for key variables, and stage assignment was achieved in all cases. Respiratory adverse events were observed in 16.9% of children; descriptive analysis showed an event rate of 25.0% during Stage 2, 25.0% during Stage 3, and 11.6% during Stage 4. CONCLUSIONS: While stage assignment was possible among captured cases, the predefined data capture targets were not met. This pilot study successfully identified key workflow and feasibility barriers, which establish a foundation for refining protocols in the upcoming multicenter ExPEDIA registry. items.title: Sugammadex interference with serum progesterone measurement: an in-vitro study.
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Sugammadex may interfere with serum progesterone immunoassays, potentially rendering measured concentrations and resulting recommendations unreliable. METHODS: We investigated the effect of a range of sugammadex concentrations on serum progesterone concentrations in samples from pre-menopausal female volunteers. Samples were spiked with sugammadex concentrations (15-120 μM), corresponding to clinical doses between 2 mg.kg-1 and 19 mg.kg-1. Total progesterone concentrations in each sample were determined using the routine electrochemiluminescence immunoassay method. A subgroup of 15 samples underwent further testing using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectroscopy, comparing baseline with sugammadex 120 μM. RESULTS: Thirty-five participants provided blood samples. Increasing concentrations of sugammadex were associated with lower measured serum progesterone, with an approximate 10% reduction with each doubling of sugammadex concentration (F(2,30) = 4.86, p = 0.015). Overall, progesterone concentrations decreased by a mean (SD) of 34.6% (12.4%) between control samples and those spiked with sugammadex 120 μM (p = 0.015). In contrast, liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectroscopy showed no statistically significant biochemical change in progesterone concentrations between baseline and sugammadex 120 μM. DISCUSSION: Sugammadex produced a dose-dependent reduction in the progesterone concentrations when measured by immunoassay techniques, but not by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectroscopy. This suggests that an immunoassay interference occurs across clinically relevant doses. Progesterone results from routine laboratory testing should be interpreted with caution in the presence of sugammadex. items.title: Psychometric Evaluation of the Turkish Version of the Induction Compliance Checklist in Children Undergoing Mask Anesthesia.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Many children undergoing anesthesia commonly exhibit distress behaviors such as anxiety, crying, and physical resistance. Assessment of this behavior is important as it could lead to postoperative behavioral changes and delayed recovery. AIM: The aim of this study was to evaluate the content validity, construct validity, internal consistency, and inter-observer reliability of the Turkish version of the Induction Compliance Checklist (ICC), which was developed to assess compliance behaviors in children during anesthesia induction. METHODS: The study was planned as a prospective observational study. Following translation of the original ICC, content validity was examined using the Davis technique with the opinions of 10 experts. Next, Turkish ICC was applied simultaneously and independently by three independent observers during mask induction to 184 children (ASA I-III) aged 1-7 years undergoing anesthesia and surgery. Inter-observer reliability was evaluated with Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC) and Fleiss Kappa/Gwet's AC1; internal consistency with KR-20 and McDonald's omega; and construct validity with single-factor confirmatory factor analysis (WLSMV). Item analysis was performed with a tetrachoric correlation matrix, floor and ceiling effects. RESULTS: Content validity was excellent (I-CVI 0.90-1.00, S-CVI≈0.99). Inter-observer reliability for the total score was excellent: InCC (1, 2) = 0.92 (95% CI: 0.90-0.94), InCC (2, 3) = 0.97 (95% CI: 0.96-0.98). At the item level, Gwet's AC1 values ranged from 0.81 to 0.97, while Kappa values were generally 0.75-0.90 except for M11. Internal consistency was at an acceptable level with KR-20 0.49-0.52 and McDonald's omega 0.66-0.82. These results are low due to the floor effect caused by premedication. Confirmatory factor analysis moderately supported the single-factor structure (best fit in Observer Surgeon: CFI = 0.927, TLI = 0.907). High floor effect was prominent especially in rarely observed severe behaviors (M7-M11); strong correlation was observed between M9-M10 (0.89-0.94). CONCLUSIONS: Following rigorous analysis, we found that the Turkish ICC is a reliable and valid tool that can assess children's compliance behaviors during pediatric anesthesia induction. items.title: Anesthesia and the Periprocedural Management of Large Vessel Occlusion Stroke Treated with Mechanical Thrombectomy: A Narrative Review.
items.abstract: Mechanical thrombectomy is the standard of care for acute ischemic stroke due to large vessel occlusion and has markedly improved functional outcomes. While procedural sedation was historically favored instead of general anesthesia due to safety concerns, current evidence does not support superior functional outcomes with procedural sedation compared with protocol-driven general anesthesia. General anesthesia is associated with higher reperfusion rates; however, strict hemodynamic control-particularly avoidance of hypotension-and ventilatory management are critical to preserving cerebral perfusion and improving outcomes. Ongoing trials are expected to clarify optimal anesthetic strategies in both anterior and posterior circulation strokes. In the meantime, the choice between general anesthesia and procedural sedation should consider patient-specific characteristics, procedural complexity, and institutional expertise. Future research should focus on better defining patient selection or stroke subtypes most likely to benefit from general anesthesia or procedural sedation, hemodynamic management, and neuroprotective strategies to maximize reperfusion, minimize complications, and improve recovery.

items.title: Rapid sequence induction: a narrative review.
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Pulmonary aspiration of gastric contents remains an important cause of anaesthetic morbidity and mortality, and is important medicolegally. Rapid sequence induction is a multi-element technique designed to mitigate risk in those patients at increased risk of pulmonary aspiration during induction of general anaesthesia. METHODS: We undertook a narrative review to summarise evidence and evidence gaps focusing on controversial aspects of rapid sequence induction. RESULTS: Despite widespread use of rapid sequence induction, many elements of the technique lack robust evidence and consensus. Nasogastric tubes can be used to reduce gastric content, but do not empty the stomach reliably. Correctly applied cricoid force obstructs the hypopharynx and has a limited impact on airway management, but incorrect application can cause clinically significant difficulties. Correct location of cricoid force may require ultrasound localisation of the cricoid cartilage. Applying the correct force, which varies with age and sex, is improved by education, practice and feedback. The use of videolaryngoscopy during rapid sequence induction is supported by evidence. The role of gastric ultrasound in determining anaesthetic technique is uncertain. Cardiovascular complications of rapid sequence induction are common, particularly in the patients who are critically ill, and modifications to the technique may reduce their frequency and severity. Effective use of airway rescue techniques may require removal of cricoid force. DISCUSSION: There is insufficient evidence for many of the elements of rapid sequence induction to determine whether they reduce patient harm or to state confidently that they do not. Controversies and evidence gaps should be acknowledged. Despite this, optimal use of rapid sequence induction requires a thorough knowledge of the subject, including areas of uncertainty to guide individualised risk assessment; clinical decision-making; and practical conduct of the technique. items.title: Recognizing Strokes in the Post-Anesthesia Care Unit in Adult Versus Pediatric Patients.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Postoperative strokes can occur in adult and pediatric patients, with both ischemic and hemorrhagic etiologies. Unfortunately, it can be difficult to distinguish stroke symptoms from lingering anesthetic-related neurological effects. Even though there is currently no standardized screening tool, a systematic approach to symptomatic differentiation between anesthetic effects and stroke symptoms can help ensure early diagnosis of a stroke and thus minimize both morbidity and mortality. AIMS: This review aims to provide an overview of perioperative stroke in pediatric and adult patients, including epidemiology, clinical presentation, and risk factors, as well as an approach to differentiating suspected stroke from anesthetic-related neurological effects in the post-anesthesia care unit (PACU). DISCUSSION: In addition to symptomatology, stroke recognition in the PACU may be facilitated by incorporating consideration of the many perioperative stroke risk factors including surgery type, medications, and both modifiable and non-modifiable patient risk factors. While PACU strokes are rare, any delay in diagnosis and thus treatment can exacerbate adverse outcomes, so it remains important to maintain suspicion of stroke in patients with concerning symptoms and risk factors. CONCLUSIONS: This focused review discusses stroke etiology, its varying risk factors and symptomatology in pediatric and adult patients, and appropriate steps to take when confronted with concerning neurological symptoms in the PACU.

items.title: Preoperative Oral Esketamine for Perioperative Comfort in Children Undergoing Adenotonsillectomy: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Dose-Finding Study.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Pediatric adenotonsillectomy often causes preoperative anxiety, venous cannulation pain, and emergence agitation. Esketamine has multimodal properties, but the optimal oral dose for children is unknown. This study evaluated oral esketamine at 1, 2, and 3 mg/kg for perioperative comfort. METHODS: In this randomized double-blind trial, 99 children (ASA I-II, 1-6 years) received oral 10% glucose (control, n = 26) or esketamine 1 mg/kg (EK1, n = 26), 2 mg/kg (EK2, n = 23), or 3 mg/kg (EK3, n = 24) 30 min before anesthesia. PRIMARY OUTCOMES: Ramsay Sedation Scale (RSS) and FLACC pain score at venous cannulation, and PAED score at 15 min after extubation. SECONDARY OUTCOMES: remifentanil use, postoperative FLACC (2-48 h), sleep quality, and adverse events. RESULTS: All esketamine doses improved sedation and analgesia at cannulation (overall p < 0.001), with largest effect at 3 mg/kg. Median RSS (IQR): control 1.00 (1.00-2.00); EK1 2.00 (1.75-3.00, p = 0.028); EK2 2.00 (1.00-3.00, p = 0.049); EK3 3.00 (2.00-3.37, p < 0.001). FLACC scores: control 6.00 (3.00-7.00); EK1 2.50 (1.00-4.00, p = 0.016); EK2 2.00 (0.00-4.00, p = 0.001); EK3 0.00 (0.00-1.75, p < 0.001). PAED score at 15 min was lower in EK2 than control (5.00 [2.00-10.00] vs. 10.00 [6.00-12.00], p = 0.048). Remifentanil consumption was reduced in EK3 (120.00 [80.00-159.50] vs. 240.00 [160.00-315.00] μg, p = 0.001). Postoperative pain at 2-6 h was lower in EK2 and EK3 (p < 0.05), persisting to 48 h in EK3 (p < 0.05). Sleep quality improved in EK3 at 24 h (p = 0.023) and 48 h (p = 0.032). Adverse events did not differ significantly. CONCLUSIONS: Preoperative oral esketamine (1-3 mg/kg) enhances perioperative comfort in children undergoing adenotonsillectomy. The 2 mg/kg dose offers the best balance of efficacy and safety, while 3 mg/kg provides superior analgesia and opioid sparing.

items.title: EEG-Guided Sevoflurane Anesthesia and Emergence Delirium in Children: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: In pediatric anesthesia, minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) guides inhalational agent dosing but may not accurately reflect anesthetic depth. EEG-guided anesthesia has shown benefits in adults but remains underused in children. AIMS: This study aims to evaluate the effect of EEG-guided anesthesia with SedLine on emergence delirium (ED) and sevoflurane dose in behaviorally noncompliant children undergoing dental procedures under general anesthesia. METHODS: In this prospective, randomized controlled trial, 100 children aged 4-10 years were randomized to standard anesthesia guided by MAC and conventional clinical signs (standard group) or EEG-guided anesthesia titrated to SedLine parameters (primary target: PSI 25-50; secondary parameter: SEF 10-15 Hz) (EEG-S group). Primary outcome was ED incidence assessed by the Pediatric Anesthesia Emergence Delirium Scale (PAEDS). Secondary outcomes included mean EtSevo values, postoperative pain, rescue analgesia, nausea/vomiting, recovery time. RESULTS: Median PAEDS scores during the first 120 min postoperatively were significantly lower in the EEG-S group compared with the Standard group (e.g., upon arrival to PACU: 4 [IQR 4] vs. 8 [IQR 4.5]). In addition, the incidence of ED upon arrival in the recovery room was significantly lower in the EEG-S group (17% vs. 43%) and at 10 min postoperatively (17% vs. 37%). The mean end-tidal sevoflurane concentration was statistically lower in the EEG-S group (maintenance EtSevo 1.88 ± 0.25 vs. 1.98 ± 0.20; mean difference = 0.10, 95% confidence interval: 0.006-0.190; p = 0.036). Postoperative FLACC pain scores were also lower in the EEG-S group, representing a potential confounding factor for ED outcomes. CONCLUSION: EEG-guided anesthesia was associated with lower PAEDS scores and reduced sevoflurane consumption compared with standard management. However, given small EEG-derived differences and potential confounding by postoperative pain, these findings should be interpreted cautiously. Within the applied target ranges, EEG-derived parameters were not independently associated with ED, and specific EEG targets predictive of ED could not be identified. TRIAL REGISTRATION: This study was registered (Protocol Registration Receipt NCT06400706/OKocaturk/May 02 2024) at http://www. CLINICALTRIAL: gov.

items.title: Automated Versus Manual Endotracheal Tube Cuff Pressure Control in Mechanically Ventilated Children: A Randomized Crossover Trial.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Optimal endotracheal tube cuff pressure is key for airway sealing and minimizing microaspiration and tracheal injury in ventilated children. However, intermittent manual monitoring can allow significant pressure changes and be affected by measurement artifacts, potentially reducing airway protection. AIMS: This study evaluated whether automated cuff pressure control better maintains target pressure than manual monitoring in ventilated children, and assessed its effects on off-target pressure and workload. METHODS: In this prospective, randomized crossover study, mechanically ventilated pediatric patients (1 month-18 years) expected to require ventilation for ≥ 48 h underwent two randomized 24-h monitoring phases (manual and automated). During the manual phase, cuff pressure was continuously displayed via a closed system without repeated disconnection of the manometer and was intermittently adjusted by bedside nurses according to a predefined protocol. During the automated phase, cuff pressure was continuously regulated using an automated control system to maintain a target range of 15-25 cmH2O. The primary outcomes were the frequency and cumulative duration of off-target cuff pressure exposure; secondary outcomes included nursing workload. RESULTS: Thirty-two patients completed both phases (768 measurements). Low cuff pressure episodes (< 15 cmH2O) were more frequent during manual monitoring than automated monitoring (12.7% vs. 1.3%, p < 0.001), while high-pressure episodes (> 25 cmH2O) occurred only during manual monitoring (2.6% vs. 0%, p < 0.001). Total time outside the target range was markedly reduced with automated monitoring (118 vs. 10 h, p < 0.001). Nursing workload was significantly lower in the automated phase (3.65 h vs. 0.08 h, p < 0.001). CONCLUSIONS: Automated cuff pressure control more reliably maintains target pressure and minimizes clinically important deviations compared to manual management. These results support adopting continuous automated regulation as a preferred strategy to enhance airway safety and reduce workload in mechanically ventilated children. items.title: Surgical wound infiltration with liposomal bupivacaine admixture as an adjunct to intrathecal morphine for post-caesarean analgesia: a randomised, double-blind controlled trial.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Intrathecal morphine is the gold standard for post-caesarean analgesia, but it lasts only 18-24 h. Whether wound infiltration adds benefit in patients receiving intrathecal morphine remains controversial. This study evaluated the opioid-sparing efficacy of wound infiltration with a liposomal bupivacaine-bupivacaine hydrochloride admixture as an adjunct to intrathecal morphine. METHODS: In this double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 188 patients undergoing elective caesarean delivery with intrathecal morphine (100 μg) received either wound infiltration with liposomal bupivacaine (266 mg) plus bupivacaine hydrochloride (100 mg), or saline placebo. All patients received standardised multimodal analgesia including scheduled non-opioid analgesics and hydromorphone patient-controlled analgesia. The primary outcome was cumulative opioid consumption (oral morphine milligram equivalents) at 48 h. RESULTS: With treatment, 48-h opioid consumption was significantly lower (12.60 mg [IQR 6.30-15.80] vs. 15.75 mg [IQR 9.45-25.50]; Hodges-Lehmann estimate -3.05 mg, 95% CI -5.9 to -1.4; P = 0.002). Secondary outcomes also favoured treatment: 24-h opioid consumption (6.30 vs. 9.45 mg; P < 0.001), movement-evoked pain at 24 h (40 vs. 50 mm; P < 0.001) and 48 h (30 vs. 40 mm; P < 0.001), time to first analgesic request (14.5 vs. 9.5 h; P < 0.001), and opioid-free status at 48 h (19.1% vs. 2.1%; RR 9.0; 95% CI 2.1-37.8; P < 0.001). CONCLUSIONS: In women undergoing scheduled caesarean delivery, wound infiltration with a liposomal bupivacaine-bupivacaine hydrochloride admixture significantly reduced postoperative opioid consumption and improved pain scores. It may be an effective opioid-sparing adjunct to intrathecal morphine.

items.title: Pediatric Postoperative Acute Kidney Injury After Noncardiac Surgery: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Postoperative acute kidney injury (AKI) is associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. Reliable estimates of AKI after surgery in children are lacking. To address this gap, we aimed to synthesize the available evidence on the incidence of AKI after pediatric noncardiac surgery. METHODS: We searched PubMed, Cochrane and Web of Science for studies reporting the incidence of AKI, defined according to the Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) criteria, within 7 postoperative days. Observational studies and clinical trials including patients aged < 18 years were eligible. The review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, and certainty of evidence was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach. RESULTS: Twenty-seven studies (n = 21 908) were included. Considerable heterogeneity (I2 = 98.7%) and likely overrepresentation of clinically distinct high-risk populations limited the interpretability of a single overall pooled incidence estimate. The incidence was 22.3% (95% CI, 11.2-39.3) after neonatal surgery, 30.1% (95% CI, 21.4-40.6) after pediatric liver transplantation, and 9.2% (95% CI, 3.3-23.6) in mixed pediatric surgical populations. The certainty of evidence was rated low to very low. In mixed pediatric surgical populations, AKI incidence increased from 2.4% in American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) class 1-2 to 7.5% in ASA 3 (p < 0.001) and 18.9% in ASA 4-5 (p < 0.001), and decreased from 9.8% at 0-2 years to 4.0% at 12-18 years (p < 0.001). CONCLUSION: The reported incidence of postoperative AKI in children undergoing noncardiac surgery remains uncertain due to substantial heterogeneity and overrepresentation of high-risk populations. AKI incidence was high in neonates and liver transplant recipients and was associated with younger age and higher ASA class, although data were limited. Further prospective studies in broader pediatric surgical populations are needed to better assess the risk of postoperative AKI in children. TRIAL REGISTRATION: PROSPERO registration no.: CRD42024518832.

items.title: Pre-Extubation Low-Dose Propofol in Pediatric Ear, Nose, and Throat Procedures: A Meta-Analysis With Trial Sequential Analysis.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Post-extubation emergence agitation (EA) is common in pediatric ear, nose, and throat (ENT) procedures and may lead to serious complications. AIMS: To assess the efficacy of low-dose propofol administered before extubation, compared with placebo, for preventing EA, using meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis (TSA). METHODS: We searched PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing low-dose propofol versus placebo administered before extubation in pediatric ENT procedures. The primary outcomes were laryngospasm, severity of EA, assessed by the Pediatric Anesthesia Emergence Delirium (PAED) scale score, and incidence of EA. Secondary outcomes included post-anesthesia care unit (PACU) length of stay, time to recovery, and time to extubation. Random-effects models were used to pool effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). TSA was performed for all outcomes to assess the robustness of the evidence. RESULTS: Ten RCTs were included in the review, of which six (414 pediatric patients) contributed to the meta-analysis. Compared with control, propofol significantly reduced the incidence of EA (risk ratio [RR] = 0.57; 95% CI, 0.42-0.78) and lowered agitation severity (mean difference [MD] = -3.94; 95% CI, -5.74 to -2.13). Time to extubation was slightly longer (MD = 1.8 min; 95% CI, 1.4-2.3), whereas time to recovery (MD = 0.9 min; 95% CI, -1.9 to 3.6) and PACU length of stay (MD = -0.63 min; 95% CI, -3.2 to 1.9) did not differ. TSA confirmed the robustness of the findings for incidence of EA, severity of EA, and time to extubation. However, the certainty of evidence was very low for severity of EA and moderate for EA incidence and time to extubation. Laryngospasm outcomes were not pooled due to substantial heterogeneity. CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that pre-extubation propofol probably reduces the incidence of EA in pediatric ENT surgery, supported by moderate-certainty evidence, and may lower EA severity measured by PAED scale scores, for which the certainty of evidence was very low. Propofol was also associated with a slightly longer time to extubation, with no difference in overall recovery time or PACU length of stay.

items.title: Effects of Esketamine on Emergence Delirium in Children Undergoing Sevoflurane Anesthesia: A Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis, and Trial Sequential Analysis.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Emergence delirium is a frequent and distressing postoperative complication in children, particularly following sevoflurane-based anesthesia. Despite its clinical importance, the optimal preventive strategy remains under investigation. This study aims to systematically evaluate the efficacy and safety of esketamine in preventing emergence delirium in pediatric patients undergoing sevoflurane-based general anesthesia. METHODS: We systematically searched seven databases and registries through 27 March 2026. Randomized controlled trials that compared esketamine with placebo in children undergoing surgical procedures were included. The primary outcome was the incidence of emergence delirium. Secondary outcomes were postoperative pain scores, extubation time, post-anesthesia care unit stay, and postoperative nausea and vomiting. Data were synthesized using random-effects models, with risk ratios for dichotomous outcomes and mean differences or standardized mean differences for continuous outcomes. Meta-regression and trial sequential analysis were performed. The risk of bias was assessed using the revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomized trials, and the certainty of the evidence was evaluated using the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation approach. RESULTS: Eight randomized controlled trials involving 916 patients were included. Esketamine significantly reduced the incidence of emergence delirium versus placebo (risk ratio = 0.35; 95% confidence interval: 0.26-0.48; p < 0.0001). No significant differences were observed between dosing regimens, surgical types, routes of administration, or timing of administration. Pain scores were significantly lower with esketamine (standardized mean difference = -0.58; 95% confidence interval: -0.79 to -0.37; p < 0.0001). Extubation time was modestly prolonged (mean difference = 1.72 min; 95% confidence interval: 0.20-3.24; p = 0.0267). Meta-regression revealed a statistically significant association between emergence delirium risk ratios and anesthesia duration (β = 0.98, p = 0.042), with no other significant associations observed for the other covariates. Post-anesthesia care unit stay showed no statistically significant difference, while postoperative nausea and vomiting was significantly reduced with esketamine (risk ratio = 0.69; 95% confidence interval: 0.49-0.97; p = 0.0304). items.title: Anesthesia Teleconsultation for Pediatric Preoperative Assessment: A Large National Prospective Multicentric Study in Children (TeleCCCAP).
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: While interest in pediatric anesthesia teleconsultation is growing, published data remain scarce. This study evaluated the feasibility of anesthesia teleconsultation in children, providing a comprehensive analysis of failure, quality, dedicated time, and satisfaction. METHODS: This prospective observational study was performed in 11 major French hospitals. The primary outcome was anesthesia teleconsultation feasibility. Feasibility was defined as the rate of successful anesthesia teleconsultations, i.e ., those performed in the presence of both child and parent, exclusively via the dedicated secure audiovisual platform, and not requiring a complementary in-person appointment. Secondary outcomes included causes and consequences of failure, factors associated with failure, quality of anesthetic preparation, medical time dedicated to preoperative assessment, analysis of parents, and anesthetist satisfaction. RESULTS: A total of 830 children aged 6.7 [25th, 75th percentiles, 3.5,12.2] yr were included. Feasibility of anesthesia teleconsultation was 73%. Failure was due to technical (91%), organizational (9%), and medical (1%) issues. Three anesthesia teleconsultations (0.4%) were converted to in-person consultations. Factors associated with technical failure included the use of tablets or smartphones rather than computers (odds ratio, 2.44; 95% CI, 1.40 to 4.26; P = 0.002), the absence of a preconnection test (odds ratio, 6.21; 95% CI, 3.05 to 12.66; P < 0.001), and several sociodemographic characteristics. On the day of surgery, no procedure was canceled, one was postponed, and one anesthetic strategy was modified. Medical time dedicated to preoperative evaluation was 28 [18,33] min. Parental satisfaction was high: 93% would choose teleconsultation for a future procedure. Anesthetists' satisfaction was high: 96% with medical aspects, 90% with the suitability for the case, and 72% with the quality of information delivered. Technical failure consistently impacted all components of anesthetist satisfaction. CONCLUSIONS: This national audit highlights that addressing technical and organizational issues appears essential to transform anesthesia teleconsultations from a mere tool into a robust clinical process, ensuring its reliability and clinical utility in pediatric anesthesia.

items.title: Volume Guarantee Versus Manual Tidal Volume Monitoring During High-Frequency Oscillatory Ventilation in Neonates: A Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial.
items.abstract: OBJECTIVE: The present study compared the effects of high-frequency oscillatory ventilation (HFOV) with automated volume guarantee (HFOV-VG) versus careful manual high-frequency tidal volume (VThf) monitoring (HFOV-VM) on the incidences of hypo/hypercarbia in neonates. METHODS: In this open-labeled, parallel-group randomized controlled trial, 60 neonates failing conventional mechanical ventilation were allocated to receive HFOV-VG (n = 30) versus HFOV-VM (n = 30) as a rescue mode. The primary outcome was the incidence of hypo/hypercarbia at 1 h. Secondary outcomes were incidences of hypo/hypercarbia at 6/12/24/48 h and beyond, time-specific trends for partial pressure of carbon dioxide (pCO2), delivered VThf and mean airway pressure (MAP), cerebral blood flow (CBF) in the anterior cerebral artery (ACA) and regional cerebral oxygenation (CrSO2), duration of respiratory support, and incidences of in-hospital adverse events. Stata 18 was used for an intention-to-treat analysis. RESULTS: The incidence of hypo- or hypercarbia at 1 h of intervention was 15/30 (50%) in the HFOV-VG and 13/30 (43%) in the HFOV-VM groups (p = 0.61). No differences were observed in the incidences of hypo- or hypercarbia anytime during HFOV. Time-specific pCO2, VThf, and MAP were similar. On regression analysis, the only significant predictor for pCO2 at 1 h was the baseline pCO2 level in both the groups. No difference was observed in ACA-CBF, CrSO2, duration of respiratory support, and in-hospital adverse events including mortality. CONCLUSION: There was no difference in the incidence of hypo/hypercarbia with HFOV-VG versus HFOV-VM at 1 h and throughout the duration of ventilation with a similar rate of complications when used as a rescue therapy. TRIAL REGISTRATION: Clinical trial registry of India, Registration no: CTRI/2024/09/073455, Registered prospectively on 05/09/2024, https://ctri.icmr.org.in/.

items.title: Perioperative Outcomes in Stage 1 Palliated Infants Undergoing Noncardiac Procedures: A Comparison by Shunt Type.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Interstage infants with single-ventricle (SV) physiology following Stage I palliation represent a high-risk population for noncardiac procedures requiring anesthesia. Data comparing perioperative outcomes by shunt type remain limited. AIMS: Describe anesthetic management, perioperative complications, and postoperative outcomes in interstage SV infants undergoing noncardiac interventions and compare outcomes between right ventricle-to-pulmonary artery (Sano) and modified Blalock-Taussig-Thomas shunt (mBTTS) patients. METHODS: We performed a retrospective single-center cohort study of interstage SV infants with Stage I palliation undergoing noncardiac surgery or nonsurgical procedures requiring anesthesia between 2015 and 2023. Outcomes were stratified by shunt type. RESULTS: A total of 208 noncardiac interventions in 120 interstage SV infants were analyzed; 136 (65.4%) encounters in 86 Sano patients and 72 (34.6%) encounters in 34 mBTTS patients. Compared with mBTTS infants, Sano patients underwent interventions at a younger age (57 [IQR 40-83] vs. 105 [59-278] days, p < 0.001) and lower weight (3.6 [3.0-4.1] vs. 4.8 [3.4-7.3] kg, p < 0.001). mBTTS procedures had higher rates of ventricular dysfunction (34.3% vs. 12.7%, p < 0.001), chromosomal abnormalities (63.9% vs. 19.1%, p < 0.001), gastrointestinal comorbidities (87.5% vs. 72.1%, p = 0.014), and hematologic comorbidities (41.7% vs. 22.8%, p = 0.006). Hemodynamic instability requiring vasoactive support was the most common perioperative complication and occurred similarly between groups (31.9% mBTTS vs. 31.6% Sano, p = 0.962). There were no perioperative cardiac arrests. Rates of postoperative escalation of care (2.9%), reintubation (3.0% vs. 2.9%, p = 0.999), readmission (16.2% vs. 16.9%, p = 0.999), and 30-day mortality (2.3% vs. 2.9%, p = 0.999) were low and comparable between groups. CONCLUSIONS: Despite the high-risk physiology of interstage SV patients, perioperative outcomes were comparable between Sano and mBTTS cohorts. However, these findings should be interpreted cautiously and should not imply low procedural risk. Favorable outcomes likely reflect careful patient selection, multidisciplinary perioperative care, and specialized institutional expertise.

items.title: Comparing Subglottic Ultrasound and Distal Phalanx Width for Pediatric Endotracheal Tube Sizing in a Predominantly School-Aged Pediatric Cohort: A Prospective Study.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Accurate endotracheal tube (ETT) sizing is essential in pediatric airway management to optimize ventilation and reduce complications. Traditional methods, including age-based formulas and distal phalanx width (DPW), may lack precision. Subglottic ultrasound (US) has emerged as a promising tool, but its predictive accuracy compared with DPW remains unclear. This study aimed to compare accuracy, agreement, diagnostic performance, and clinical applicability of subglottic US versus DPW for predicting optimal ETT size in children, while recognizing that the enrolled cohort was predominantly school-aged. METHODS: In this prospective observational study, pediatric patients aged 0-12 years undergoing elective or emergency intubation were assessed. Pre-intubation measurements included subglottic transverse airway diameter by ultrasound (ACUSON Juniper, microconvex probe, 5-10 MHz) and DPW by digital calipers. Predicted ETT sizes were compared with the final clinically accepted cuffed ETT inner diameter confirmed by leak testing and cuff pressure optimization. Agreement was evaluated using Bland-Altman analysis and intraclass correlation coefficients, while diagnostic performance was defined a priori as accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), likelihood ratios, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis. Logistic regression identified predictors of good ETT fit. RESULTS: Among 160 patients, the median age was 8.8 years (IQR 7.0-10.5), indicating predominance of older children. Ultrasound-predicted ETT size showed a stronger correlation with actual size (r = 0.479, p < 0.001) than DPW (r = 0.248, p = 0.002). Ultrasound predictions had narrower Bland-Altman limits of agreement, although ultrasound measurement is operator-dependent. DPW showed poor sensitivity (5.9%) but high specificity (99.3%) for identifying underfit ETTs, with limited overall discrimination (ROC AUC = 0.53). Only subglottic diameter was a significant predictor of good ETT fit. CONCLUSION: Subglottic ultrasound showed better agreement with clinically accepted ETT size than DPW in this predominantly school-aged pediatric cohort. These findings support the potential role of ultrasound as an adjunct to pediatric airway assessment, but conclusions should be interpreted cautiously in infants and younger children because they were under-represented. Standardized measurement protocols and operator training are needed

items.title: Frequency of Adherence to Obstetric Anesthesia Best Practices for Cesarean Delivery: A Multicenter Retrospective Cohort Analysis.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Increasingly, protocols have been developed to optimize obstetric anesthesia care. However, there is a paucity of data on adherence to these guidelines. The primary aims of this study were to utilize the Multicenter Perioperative Outcomes Group (MPOG) database to estimate (1) the rate of adherence to best practice guidelines for cesarean delivery, (2) the association of case- and hospital-level factors with adherence, and (3) the percentage of variability in adherence attributable to the patient-, case-, and hospital-level factors. METHODS: The authors performed a multicenter observational cohort study utilizing the MPOG database to review all cesarean deliveries in women age 15 to 44 yr. Best practices were defined based on societal guidelines and included timely antibiotic administration, postspinal systolic blood pressure (SBP) maintenance greater than 90 mmHg, general anesthesia avoidance, prevention of perioperative hypothermia, use of low-dose neuraxial morphine, postspinal vasopressor infusions, and spinal needles 25-gauge or smaller. Covariates of interest included patient-, case-, and hospital-level factors. RESULTS: The authors analyzed 289,047 cesarean delivery cases in the MPOG database from 2015 to 2022. The following adherence outcomes were observed: timely antibiotic administration, 86.2% (99% CI, 86 to 86.3%); postspinal SBP maintenance, 96.7% (99% CI, 96.6 to 96.8%); avoidance of general anesthesia, 97.0% (99% CI, 96.9 to 97.0%); prevention of perioperative hypothermia, 56.7% (99% CI, 56.5 to 56.9%); use of low-dose neuraxial morphine, 74.2% (99% CI, 74.0 to 74.5%); use of postspinal vasopressor infusion, 55.4% (99% CI, 55.1 to 55.8%); and use of 25-gauge needle or smaller for spinal anesthesia, 89.0% (99% CI, 88.6 to 89.4%). Poorer adherence correlated with factors at the patient level (American Society of Anesthesiologists [Schaumburg, Illinois] Physical Status IV or greater), case level (evening or overnight cesarean delivery), and institution level (absence of obstetric fellowship or Center of Excellence status). CONCLUSIONS: Among this large cohort of cesarean delivery cases, overall adherence to guideline-supported best practices was variable, with postspinal vasopressor infusions being the lowest and avoidance of general anesthesia being the highest. Targeted interventions addressing these factors may improve quality and promote more optimal care.

items.title: Project SPRUCE: Formation of an International Consortium of Pediatric Anesthesia Groups to Reduce Greenhouse Gas Emissions from Inhaled Anesthetics.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Inhaled anesthetic use contributes to environmental harm through release of potent greenhouse gases (GHG). Emissions can be reduced with the use of safe practice changes, including avoidance of high impact agents like desflurane and nitrous oxide, use of low fresh gas flows, and adoption of total intravenous and regional anesthesia when clinically appropriate. These evidence-based practices have been recommended for years, but actual practice changes have not been widely adopted. METHODS: The Project SPRUCE (Saving our Planet by Reducing Carbon Emissions) consortium brought together twelve pediatric anesthesia groups into a partnership working to reduce GHG emissions from pediatric anesthesia care. The consortium implemented quality improvement strategies, including change management methods, to reduce GHG emissions from inhaled anesthetics by at least 50%. Change management and quality improvement strategies were utilized to disseminate strategies, implement emissions reduction techniques, and track emissions in pediatric anesthesia care. Specific interventions included education and socialization, practice constraints, and direct data feedback to clinical teams. RESULTS: The consortium facilitated adoption of practice changes among anesthesia groups, and sustained emissions reductions though shifts in culture. Greenhouse gas emissions from inhaled anesthesia decreased by 63% (range 43-91%) During the study period, the incidence of nitrous oxide use was reduced by 62.4%, and the average volume of nitrous oxide used per case decreased by 83.5%. Project SPRUCE prevented a total of 14,381 metric tons of excess carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2e) emissions from inhaled anesthetics. CONCLUSIONS: Collaborative action within our consortium supported widespread and significant reductions in harmful greenhouse gas emissions from pediatric anesthesia care through education and socialization, practice constraints, and direct data feedback to clinical teams.

items.title: Complications in neonates with difficult tracheal intubation: an analysis of the Pediatric Difficult Intubation Registry.
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Difficult tracheal intubation is associated with serious complications, including hypoxia, bradycardia and cardiac arrest. Neonates have increased physiologic vulnerability compared with older children, yet detailed data on management strategies and outcomes in neonates with difficult tracheal intubation remain limited. We hypothesised that clinicians have lower first-attempt tracheal intubation success and higher complication rates for neonates compared with older children with difficult tracheal intubation. METHODS: We analysed the Pediatric Difficult Intubation Registry to determine tracheal intubation first attempt success and incidence of complications. We used logistic regression to identify variables associated with complications in neonates. RESULTS: During the study period, 6283 paediatric difficult tracheal intubations were recorded, including 420 neonates. First attempt success was lower for neonates (139/420, 33.1%) than older children (2394/4683, 51.1%). Complications occurred more frequently in neonates (123/420, 29.3%) than older children (637/4683, 13.6%). Hypoxia occurred in 92/420 (21.9%) neonates and 269/4683 (5.7%) older children. Severe complications were more frequent in neonates vs. older children (12/420, 2.9% vs. 30/4683, 0.6%, respectively), with cardiac arrests occurring in 4/420 (1.0%) neonates and 11/4683 (0.2%) older children. Difficult mask ventilation occurred more frequently in neonates (60/420, 14.3%) than older children (353/4681, 7.5%). In neonates, increased number of tracheal intubation attempts (aOR 1.61 per attempt, 95%CI 1.30-2.00, p < 0.001) and difficult facemask ventilation (aOR 3.17, 95%CI 1.38-7.30, p = 0.007) were associated with complications. Anticipated difficulty with airway management had a protective effect (aOR 0.37, 95%CI 0.16-0.88, p = 0.025). DISCUSSION: Neonates with difficult tracheal intubation experience a substantially higher rate of complications than older children. Early recognition of risk is critical in order to enable careful planning to minimise tracheal intubation attempts in this vulnerable population. We compared how often the tube was placed successfully on the first try and how often problems occurred in newborn babies and older children.
